notes.meaning: King Darius ordered a careful search in the royal archives of Babylon to find the original decree made by King Cyrus. The king wanted to know whether the Jews truly had official permission to rebuild their temple. His willingness to check the records kept the governors from stopping the work right away.

The searchers did not find the document in Babylon, but they discovered a scroll in the royal fortress at Ecbatana in Media. Ecbatana was the summer home of the Persian kings, which explains why the records from Cyrus were kept there. God guided the search so the vital memorandum would not be lost or overlooked.

The scroll showed that Cyrus had officially decreed that the house of God in Jerusalem must be rebuilt on its ancient foundations as a place for sacrifices. The memorandum gave permitted dimensions of sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide. This confirmed that the Jewish builders were acting under royal Persian authority from the very beginning.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars observe that the biblical text gives few physical details about the rebuilt temple beyond these dimensions, placing the main emphasis on rebuilding upon the exact site of Solomon's temple.

notes.meaning: Cyrus had ordered the temple walls to be constructed with three layers of large stones and one layer of timber. The decree also stated that the building expenses should be paid from the royal treasury. These instructions proved that the builders' materials were completely authorized by the crown.

The decree commanded that the gold and silver vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar must be returned to their proper place in Jerusalem. King Cyrus had treated these sacred items with great respect, ordering each piece restored to God's house. God preserved these precious treasures through decades of exile so His worship could be fully restored.

Darius immediately sent word back to Governor Tattenai and his fellow officials, commanding them to stay completely away from the work. The local rulers were forbidden to interfere or cause any trouble for the builders. God turned an inquiry started by suspicious officials into a royal shield of protection for His people.

Darius commanded the governors to let the Jewish elders rebuild the house of God without disturbance on its original site. The king recognized their right to worship where their fathers had worshiped. Even a pagan ruler respected the sacred ground chosen by the Lord.

The king went further by ordering that the full costs of rebuilding be paid to the Jewish elders out of the royal tax revenues collected from that very province. Instead of draining the Jewish community, the local taxes were diverted to fund the temple. In this remarkable turn of events, God provided abundant resources through the government itself.

Darius commanded that the priests in Jerusalem receive everything they needed for daily worship, including bulls, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine, and oil. These specific items were required by the Law of Moses for the morning and evening offerings. The king ordered these supplies to be delivered every single day without fail.

Darius explained his purpose for supporting the temple: he wanted the priests to offer pleasing sacrifices and pray for his life and the lives of his sons. Persian rulers believed in gaining the favor of local gods and valued the intercession of their subjects. God used this royal desire for prayer to ensure steady provision for His own house.

The decree carried a severe warning for anyone who tried to change the king's order or stop the work. A wooden beam would be pulled from the offender's own home, the person would be impaled or hanged on it, and the house would be turned into a heap of rubble. Persian law treated disobedience to the king's word as a capital crime.

Darius concluded his decree with a prayer that God, who caused His name to dwell in Jerusalem, would destroy any king or people who attempted to harm the temple. The Persian emperor acknowledged the supreme power of Israel's God over all earthly rulers. He demanded that his royal command be executed with total speed and diligence.

Governor Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai, and their officials complied at once with the king's orders. They moved swiftly to provide the funds and supplies just as Darius had commanded. The very men who had questioned the project were now actively helping to bring it to completion.

The Jewish leaders continued building and made rapid progress, encouraged by the preaching of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. The project succeeded under God's command and with the backing of the Persian kings Cyrus, Darius, and later Artaxerxes. God used both prophetic voices and royal decrees to fulfill His purpose.

The temple was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, during the sixth year of King Darius. The work reached its finish about twenty years after the first foundation had been laid under Cyrus. God's promise was fulfilled, and Jerusalem had a standing temple once again.

The priests, Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles celebrated the dedication of the temple with great joy. Dedicating the building meant setting it apart entirely for sacred use and God's worship. The sorrow of past decades gave way to shared praise and gladness.

At the dedication, the people offered hundreds of bulls, rams, and lambs, along with twelve male goats as a sin offering for all twelve tribes of Israel. A sin offering was an animal sacrifice given to ask God's forgiveness and clean away wrongdoing. Even though only a small remnant had returned from captivity, the twelve goats showed their faith that God still held all twelve tribes in His covenant.

The leaders organized the priests and Levites into their proper service groups according to the Book of Moses. They wanted the daily temple duties to be carried out in exact obedience to God's written law. A beautifully finished building meant little without faithful, orderly worship inside it.

On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles kept the Passover. This annual feast commemorated how God spared Israel's firstborn sons and brought their ancestors out of slavery in Egypt. Celebrating it in a newly finished temple reminded them that God had delivered them from bondage once again.

All the priests and Levites purified themselves together and were ceremonially clean, meaning they completed the washing rituals needed to be fit for sacred service. Because the Levites were fully prepared, they slaughtered the Passover lambs for the priests, the people, and themselves. Their unity and purity made the entire feast orderly and holy.

The Passover meal was shared by the returned exiles and by everyone who had separated from the unclean, immoral ways of the surrounding people to seek the Lord. God welcomed anyone who turned away from false gods to worship Him in truth. True fellowship among God's people was based on devotion to the Lord rather than mere heritage.

The people celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with overflowing joy. The Lord gave them this gladness by turning the heart of the Persian king to favor them and support the work on God's house. Calling the Persian ruler the king of Assyria recalled Israel's ancient oppressor and showed how God had transformed their former enemies into helpers.
